3. Does every vehicle match? Same layout, same colors, same placement, so the fleet reads as one company.

Get those three right and the rest is style.

items.title: Harbor News Through Time: The Purdy Bridge (1937)
items.caption:
Gig Harbor Through Time: The Purdy Bridge.

The Purdy Bridge was completed on Sept. 29, 1937, over the channel between Henderson Bay and Burley Lagoon. At the time it was considered the longest bridge of its kind: a reinforced-concrete box girder, a design common in Europe but rare in America. Engineer Homer Hadley suggested the design.

It runs 550 feet end to end over five spans, with a 190-foot center span, and it's the fourth bridge at this spot. Pierce County built the first one, a wooden bridge with a swing span, in 1892. Today it's on the National Register of Historic Places.

items.title: Harbor News Through Time: The Fox Island Bridge (1954)
items.caption:
Gig Harbor Through Time: The Fox Island Bridge.

On Aug. 28, 1954, Gov. Arthur B. Langlie cut the ribbon on the bridge across Hale Passage, and Fox Island traded the ferry for a road to the mainland. The Washington State Toll Bridge Authority built the 1,981-foot span, and it ran as a toll bridge until 1965. Seventy-two years later, it's still the island's road to the mainland.

Bonus fact: the island itself was named in 1841, during the Wilkes Expedition, for Dr. J.L. Fox, an assistant surgeon on the voyage.

items.title: Harbor News Through Time: Born From the Flames (Fire District No. 5, 1945)
items.caption:
Gig Harbor Through Time: Born From the Flames.

In the spring of 1944, a fire tore through the north-end waterfront and destroyed several businesses. Gig Harbor had no organized fire department, so neighbors led by John Finholm got together and started one.

By January 1945, Pierce County Fire Protection District No. 5 was official, an all-volunteer department. The first career hire came in 1973. Today that department is Gig Harbor Fire & Medic One, covering about 54 square miles of the Peninsula, Fox Island and Raft Island from nine stations.

Eighty-one years later, it's still neighbors looking out for neighbors. Thank you to every firefighter and medic, volunteer and career, who has answered the call out here.

items.title: Real job photo: gray teak cockpit
items.caption:
Gray teak-style EVA, dark seam lines, and a floor that feels good barefoot.

This cockpit floor was patterned to the boat, so every panel follows the hull edge and the cabinet instead of a generic mat trimmed to fit. Cut and finished in our Gig Harbor shop.

EVA stays softer and cooler than bare fiberglass and keeps its grip when it is wet, which matters on a Puget Sound morning.

Off-season is a good time to plan new decking. Bring your boat by the Gig Harbor shop and we will help you pick a color and layout
